flawed_step: Lines 0010-0014: the proof-by-contradiction setup assumes only 'A sorted non-decreasing, l < r, A[l]+A[r] < t' and tries to derive a contradiction from the existence of r' > r with A[l]+A[r'] = t. No contradiction is derivable: line 0012 yields A[r] < A[r'], which is fully consistent with sortedness because r' > r. The goal stated in line 0014 ('disprove the existence of some r'') is a false statement under the stated hypotheses.
counterexample: A = [1, 2, 3, 10] (sorted non-decreasing), t = 11, l = 0, r = 2. Hypotheses hold: l < r, and A[l] + A[r] = 1 + 3 = 4 < 11 = t. Yet r' = 3 > r exists with A[l] + A[r'] = 1 + 10 = 11 = t. Line 0012's derivation gives A[r] = 3 < 10 = A[r'], which is consistent with sortedness (r' > r forces A[r'] >= A[r]), so no contradiction ever arises. Hence the claim the proof sets out to establish is refuted by this instance.
reasoning_summary: The riskiest claim is the contradiction hypothesis in line 0010 together with the goal in line 0014. The write-up tries to justify the two-pointer step by showing that when A[l]+A[r] < t there can be no r' > r with A[l]+A[r'] = t. That statement is simply false for arbitrary sorted arrays and arbitrary index pairs, as A = [1,2,3,10], t = 11, l = 0, r = 2, r' = 3 shows; the only fact line 0012 extracts, A[r] < A[r'], is exactly what sortedness predicts for r' > r, so the contradiction can never be closed. The reason r' is irrelevant in the real algorithm is not sortedness but the loop invariant that every index above the current r has already been eliminated; the lemma actually needed for the sum < t branch is that l can be discarded, since for every j with l < j <= r we have A[j] <= A[r] and hence A[l]+A[j] <= A[l]+A[r] < t. The submitted argument neither states nor uses that invariant and is, by the author's own admission at line 0013, incomplete; as written its target claim is refutable.
